chunk_findings.detail: The added queue design makes each queued waiter hold an flock on its ticket file while waiting and poll every `QUEUE_POLL_S = 0.25` seconds. This violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which states agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting. With multiple CI runs queued for the full-suite lock, every queued agent polls at 4 Hz while holding a lock, which is exactly the pattern the guidance forbids.

chunk_findings.detail: The new code constructs `SuiteBusy(_holders(directory, limit), time.monotonic() - start, position)` both in the `say(...)` call and in the `raise`. The previous implementation called `SuiteBusy(holders, elapsed)` with only two arguments, and this diff does not update the `SuiteBusy` class. With any non-first waiter, the first time `position != said` it tries to build the exception and gets a `TypeError` instead of a `SuiteBusy` refusal, so the queue wait can crash before timing out or notifying.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py:hold

chunk_findings.detail: In `_live`, a `.ticket` is unlinked whenever `fsio.file_lock(path, 0)` can acquire the lock; `age` is checked only on `LockTimeout`. A new or reclaimed `.ticket` is briefly an unlocked file between the rename/open in `_Ticket.__init__`/`__enter__` and the owner actually acquiring the flock. If another waiter scans in that window, it locks and deletes the ticket. The just-created waiter then has no visible directory entry, `_beat` fails on the missing path, and later `_live` scans never include it, so it is treated as last and can be passed by later arrivals.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/suitelock.py:_live

chunk_findings.detail: When a waiter times out, `_Ticket.__exit__` renames `self.path` to `.parked` without first calling `_beat`. The parked file keeps the last heartbeat `st_mtime`, not the parking time. If the final `_live()` scan before timeout takes longer than `grace_s`, the just-created parked file is already older than `grace_s`, so the next scanner treats it as expired and deletes it, losing the kept queue place.

chunk_findings.detail: The wait `_until(lambda: _tickets(tmp_path) == 1)` is not a valid barrier here. The first `early` attempt at line 138 has already created a `.ticket` file; for the later retry to keep its place, that ticket must still exist as `*.ticket` after `SuiteBusy`. Therefore `_tickets(tmp_path)` is already `1` before `late = _waiter(...)` is started, so this wait can return immediately before `late` has actually enqueued. The following `_until(lambda: _tickets(tmp_path) == 2)` can then be satisfied by the retained `early` ticket plus `late`'s new ticket before the `early` retry thread is scheduled; the outer holder is released with only `late` ready, making `order == ["early", "late"]` flaky or failing. The condition after starting `late` should require a count that cannot be satisfied by the retained early ticket (or otherwise wait for `late` to have its own ticket), otherwise the test does not exercise the intended “retry keeps place” interleaving deterministically.

chunk_findings.detail: The new FIFO wait path violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal] (“agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting”): `QUEUE_POLL_S = 0.25` introduces a 250 ms polling loop, and the module docstring says each waiter “holds an flock on it” while queued. For example, with `max_concurrent_suites=1`, a second suite waits by polling/touching every 250 ms while retaining its ticket flock; a stopped waiter can then hold a live flock without heartbeating, forcing reliance on the added stale-timeout heuristic instead of an event-driven wakeup.

chunk_findings.detail: A newly created but not yet flocked ticket is omitted from `live` while age <= `NEW_S`; only an unlocked ticket older than `NEW_S` is unlinked. This lets a later process overtake an earlier one. Interleaving: waiter A enters `_Ticket.__enter__`, where `fsio.file_lock(path, 0)` has created `000...-a.ticket` but A is descheduled between file creation and taking the flock; waiter B then enters with a later timestamp, scans, sees A’s unlocked young ticket and neither appends nor removes it, so `line` is `[B]`, `position == 1`, and B acquires a free slot before A. The arrival order is broken.

chunk_findings.detail: The `.parked` branch unlinks any parked file older than `grace_s` without first checking whether it is currently locked for reuse. `_Ticket.__enter__` locks `self._parked` before renaming it to `.ticket`, so a scanner can unlink the parked file after that lock is acquired but before the rename. The retry then suppresses the rename `OSError` and the missing-path `_beat`, and enters `hold` with no visible ticket; `position = len(line) + 1` can make it lose the kept place. This is triggered by a retry racing with a scan after its parked ticket exceeds `grace_s`.

chunk_findings.detail: A legitimate new waiter can be aborted by the scanner. For a new ticket, `_Ticket.__init__` does not create `self.path`; `fsio.file_lock(self.path, 0)` must create and lock the file. The path is visible after creation but before the lock is held. Another waiter's `_live` can see that just-created `.ticket`, and its “created, its owner has not locked it yet” branch calls `fsio.file_lock(path, 0)` itself. If that scanner wins the flock first, the new owner's own `fsio.file_lock` then raises `fsio.LockTimeout`, which `_Ticket.__enter__` does not catch or retry. The new waiter then fails before entering the queue even though it did nothing wrong.

chunk_findings.detail: The watcher captures the owner PID with `owner = os.getppid()` when the script first runs. If the owner is SIGKILLed after `subprocess.Popen` for the watcher returns but before that first statement executes, the watcher has already been reparented, so `os.getppid()` returns PID 1 (or a subreaper). The watcher then never sees a parent change and never calls `os.killpg`, leaving the orphaned command group alive—the exact failure this code was added to fix. Passing the owner PID explicitly from the parent and checking `os.kill(owner, 0)` would close this race.

chunk_findings.detail: The watcher `Popen` handle is discarded and never waited for. The watcher starts by sleeping 1 second before its first group check, so it is still running when the temporary `Popen` object is deallocated; Python does not reap it later. After the watched group exits normally, the watcher exits and, under the normal SIGCHLD disposition, becomes a zombie child of the still-running owner. A long-lived owner that runs many shell commands leaks one zombie per completed run and can eventually exhaust the process table. chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify the whole process group is killed, but it never records the PID of the actual `sleep 600` process. chunk_findings.detail: When `_WATCHER` sees the owner is gone, it sends one `os.killpg(group, SIGKILL)` and then unconditionally `break`s, without verifying the group is actually gone. chunk_findings.detail: The fix to retry SIGKILL still does not ensure the group is gone. Concrete input: a non-root owner runs `run_shell("sudo -u nobody sleep 600")`. chunk_findings.detail: The new `_blocked_on` regex is `blocked on [^\n]+` with no word boundary, and `classify_exit` applies it to any gate and any output. chunk_findings.detail: A configured ci gate whose command already contains `--timeout` (for example, the shared-config workaround this change is meant to replace) is not overridden: the condition `"--timeout" not in command` skips the append and leaves the old value. Given `command = "ddflow ci run --timeout 7200"` and `gate run item ci --timeout 30`, `_with_run_timeout` returns `replace(gdef, timeout_s=30, command="ddflow ci run --timeout 7200")`, so the inner `ddflow ci run` still uses 7200, not the requested per-run 30, violating the stated replacement of the ci budget.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: `_with_run_timeout` dereferences `gdef.command.strip()` before `run` has rejected human/agent gates. A human gate configured with no command (`run`'s own docstring describes it as "nothing to run") can have `gdef.command is None`; `gate run <item> <human_gate> --timeout 30` then raises `AttributeError` instead of returning the documented refusal for a human gate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: `timeout_s=int(a.get("timeout") or 0)` makes an explicit `--timeout 0` / MCP `timeout: 0` indistinguishable from an omitted value; the same `or 0` coercion is used in `ddflow/surfaces/commands/ci.py:60` and `ddflow/surfaces/declared/export.py:512`. The stated contract is that the per-run timeout is bounded by `1..[gates].max_run_timeout_s`, so `0` is outside the allowed range and must be refused with exit 3. Instead the handler passes `0`, which the rest of the pipeline treats as “no override”, so `ddflow gate run <id> <gate> --timeout 0` is silently accepted and the gate runs with its own timeout rather than being refused.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle.py:433

chunk_findings.detail: `test_the_ci_gate_passes_the_budget_to_ddflow_ci_run` loads the real current-directory configuration via `Config.load(Path("."))` instead of using the isolated `repo` fixture or a constructed `Config` with known defaults. If the checkout running the test has `.ddflow/local/config.toml` with `[gates].max_run_timeout_s` set below `7200` (e.g. `60`), then `_with_run_timeout(cfg, gate, 7200, "T1", "ci")` will refuse/clamp that timeout, and the assertion `out.timeout_s == 7200` will fail. This makes the test depend on the developer’s mutable local ddflow config rather than the documented default cap.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_run_timeout_override.py:55

chunk_findings.detail: The override is only injected when `"--timeout" not in command`. If a ci gate command is already `ddflow ci run --timeout=60` (a valid form once `--timeout` exists there), then `gate run <id> ci --timeout 120` leaves the command unchanged while still replacing `gdef.timeout_s`. The inner `ddflow ci run` still uses 60s, so the per-run override does not actually replace the ci budget as the change requires.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: The stated contract is that a timeout outside `1..[gates].max_run_timeout_s` is refused with exit 3, but both checks special-case `timeout_s == 0` as “not provided”. Thus `ddflow ci run --timeout 0` and `ddflow gate run <id> <gate> --timeout 0` are accepted and run with the gate’s default timeout instead of being refused for an out-of-range value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/cirun.py:136 and ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: The new call sites collapse "timeout not provided" and an explicit `--timeout 0` to the same integer `0` via `int(getattr(a, "timeout", 0) or 0)` in `ci.py` (and the identical `int(a.get("timeout") or 0)` in `ddflow/surfaces/declared/export.py` and `ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle.py`). Since a normal invocation without `--timeout` also sends `0` as the "no override" sentinel, the run implementation cannot reject the invalid value `0`. For example, `ddflow gate run <id> <gate> --timeout 0` or `ddflow ci run --timeout 0` will be treated as if no override was supplied and the gate runs with its own timeout, instead of being refused with exit 3 as required by the specified bound `1..cap`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/ci.py:60

chunk_findings.detail: `test_the_ci_gate_passes_the_budget_to_ddflow_ci_run` calls `Config.load(Path("."))` instead of using the isolated `repo` fixture. This reads the checkout's current directory config. If a developer's/checkout's `.ddflow/local/config.toml` has `[gates].max_run_timeout_s` set below `7200` (exactly the knob this change tells users to edit), `_with_run_timeout(cfg, gate, 7200, "T1", "ci")` will either raise/refuse or return a clamped gate, so the assertions `out.timeout_s == 7200` and `other.timeout_s == 90` fail. The test should construct a default `Config` or load the temp `repo` config to be hermetic.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_run_timeout_override.py:56

chunk_findings.detail: The new `timeout_s` argument is accepted by `_ci` for both actions, but the `action == "status"` branch only rejects the run-only `base`/`command`/`ref` arguments and never checks `timeout_s`. A call such as `ddflow_ci(repo, action="status", timeout_s=0)` therefore returns the status outcome and the explicit zero is silently ignored instead of being refused, bypassing the new validation that lives only in `run`. If `timeout_s` is meaningful only for `action="run"` (it is passed only to `run`), the status branch should reject `timeout_s is not None` just as it rejects `command`; otherwise an explicit invalid timeout can pass through the `ddflow_ci` tool.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/cirun.py:_ci

chunk_findings.detail: `_with_run_timeout` always appends the replacement timeout to the end of the command, e.g. `command = re.sub(...) + f" --timeout {timeout_s}"`. For a valid ci gate command that uses `--` to pass arguments to the test command, this puts `--timeout` after the option terminator, so `ddflow ci run` itself never consumes it. Given input `gdef.command = "ddflow ci run -- pytest"` and `gate run <id> ci --timeout 120`, the function returns `"ddflow ci run -- pytest --timeout 120"`. The `--timeout 120` is passed to `pytest` rather than setting the `ddflow ci run` budget, so the per-run override does not replace the ci budget as the change requires. The same application also corrupts an inner `pytest --timeout=30` by stripping it and re-adding it after `--`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: The new test `tests/test_gate_run_timeout_override.py::test_a_ci_command_that_already_carries_a_timeout_is_overridden` only exercises a command with the space-separated form `ddflow ci run --timeout 7200`. It does not answer the prior `--timeout=60` defect: if a ci gate command is `ddflow ci run --timeout=60`, then `gate run <id> ci --timeout 120` can still leave the nested `ddflow ci run` using 60s while the outer gate def is set to 120s, because the override still keys on the space-separated `--timeout ` token rather than the valid `--timeout=60` form.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: The command cleanup regex `re.sub(r"\s--timeout(?:=|\s+)\d+", "", command)` scans the entire command string, including the part after the first `--` that is passed through to the test runner. Given a gate command like `"ddflow ci run -- pytest --timeout=30"` and `timeout_s=60`, this removes the test runner's ` --timeout=30` after the `--`, producing `"ddflow ci run --timeout 60 -- pytest"` instead of preserving the pass-through argument; this violates the stated behavior that the override goes before any `--` and changes the command the gate actually runs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: The first `re.sub` is unanchored, so it removes any ` --timeout` / ` --timeout=` token anywhere in the command, including arguments after the `--` option terminator that belong to the test runner. Given `gdef.command = "ddflow ci run -- pytest --timeout=30"` and `timeout_s=120`, line 713 returns `"ddflow ci run -- pytest"`, and the next insertion yields `"ddflow ci run --timeout 120 -- pytest"`. The test runner’s own `--timeout=30` is silently deleted even though the replacement itself is correctly placed before `--`; only the segment before the first `--` should be rewritten.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:713

chunk_findings.detail: `test_ci_status_refuses_a_timeout` supplies `timeout_s=0`. An implementation can still be broken for the intended behavior yet pass this test: if `ci_tool` honors a positive `timeout_s` for `action="status"` (the defect the test is meant to prevent), `timeout_s=0` can be refused only because `0` is not a valid timeout value, not because `ci status` refuses timeouts. A regression where `ci status --timeout 1` succeeds would remain green. Use a positive value such as `1` while asserting exit 3 (or exercise the CLI `ci status --timeout 1`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_run_timeout_override.py:104

chunk_findings.detail: Given a gate command like `"ddflow ci run --\tpytest --timeout=30"` (a literal tab after the `--` pass-through marker, which the shell treats as an argument separator) and `timeout_s=60`, `command.partition(" -- ")` does not split because it only matches the exact three-character substring `" -- "`. The first `re.sub(r"\s--timeout(?:=|\s+)\d+", "", head)` then runs over the whole command, removes the test runner’s ` --timeout=30`, and the function produces `"ddflow ci run --timeout 60 --\tpytest"` instead of preserving the pass-through timeout. The same occurs with newline-separated `--` tokens, so the intended “only the part before ` -- ` is rewritten” behavior is still violated for valid IFS whitespace other than exactly a space around `--`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_with_run_timeout

chunk_findings.detail: `new = '21600'` is a TOML string, not an integer. The `gates.max_run_timeout_s` knob is used as a seconds bound and compared against `timeout_s` values such as `120`; after this upgrade change is applied, the config value will be the string `"21600"`, so a comparison like `timeout_s > max_run_timeout_s` raises `TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'` (or schema validation rejects the knob). It should be `new = 21600`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.gates.max_run_timeout_s.toml:6

chunk_findings.detail: `doctor_notes` always emits `kill -- -{o.pgid}`. In a PID namespace where the orphaned pre-commit suite is PID 1, `o.pgid` is 1 and the note says to run `kill -- -1`. In `kill(1)`/`kill(2)`, `-1` is the special “all killable processes” pid, not process group 1: it signals every permitted process except PID 1 and the caller. If the suite is PID 1, it is exempt and keeps running while unrelated work is killed, so the note does not “end it” and is actively destructive.

chunk_findings.detail: `_is_suite` only checks that the flattened cmdline contains the substrings `pre-commit`, `--hook-stage`, `pre-push`, and `--all-files`; it does not require `pre-commit` to be the executable path or these to be separate argv tokens. For pid running `sh -c 'echo pre-commit --hook-stage pre-push --all-files; tail -f /dev/null'`, `_is_suite()` returns true, and after 600 seconds with no ddflow ancestor doctor reports it as an orphaned CI suite and advises killing its process group even though no pre-commit run exists.

chunk_findings.detail: On a host where `/proc` is unavailable (macOS, Windows, or a Linux container with procfs not mounted), this call invokes `ORPHANS.orphaned_ci_suites()`, whose stated mechanism is reading `/proc`. The nearby host-signal call is explicitly treated as non-fatal on unsupported platforms, but this new call is not guarded, so `os.listdir('/proc')` or reading `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` raises `FileNotFoundError` and aborts the entire health report instead of merely omitting orphan-suite notes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/health.py:351

chunk_findings.detail: `_is_suite` returns true whenever the flattened cmdline merely contains the substrings `"pre-commit"`, `"--hook-stage"`, `"pre-push"`, and `"--all-files"`. A long-running unrelated process such as `bash -c 'echo "pre-commit --hook-stage pre-push --all-files"; sleep 3600'` passes this check, and if it is the caller's UID, is older than 10 minutes, and has no matching ancestor, `orphaned_ci_suites` will report it and `doctor_notes` will tell the operator to `kill -- -<pgid>` for a process that is not a CI suite.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/orphan_suites.py:_is_suite

chunk_findings.detail: `_has_ddflow_ancestor` treats any ancestor whose cmdline contains the literal substring `"ddflow"` as an actual ddflow process. An orphaned suite whose parent is, for example, `bash -c 'echo ddflow; exec pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files'` and whose chain ends at init/systemd will be suppressed as having a ddflow ancestor even though no ddflow process is above it, so `orphaned_ci_suites` misses a genuine orphan and defeats the detection.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/orphan_suites.py:_has_ddflow_ancestor

chunk_findings.detail: The ancestor walk never checks PID 1 because the loop is `while pid > 1` and the parent check is also gated with `if pid > 1 and _is_ddflow(...)`. In a container whose PID 1 is ddflow itself, a suite child of that PID 1 reaches `pid = 1`, exits the loop, and returns `False`. `orphaned_ci_suites` then records it as an orphan and `doctor_notes` advises killing a live, non-orphaned suite.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/orphan_suites.py:_has_ddflow_ancestor

chunk_findings.detail: `_is_ddflow` treats any process whose first argument’s basename is `ddflow` or `ddflow-mcp` as a ddflow process because it checks `head[:2]`. For example, an ancestor argv of `/usr/bin/vim ddflow` (an editor opened on a file named `ddflow`, not a ddflow process) returns `True`. If an actually orphaned suite is a descendant of such a process, `_has_ddflow_ancestor` suppresses it and detection fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/orphan_suites.py:_is_ddflow

chunk_findings.detail: When `pre-commit` is installed normally from PyPI/pipx/uv, the executable is a shebang script. Linux execs the Python interpreter with the script path, so the real `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is `["python3", "/path/to/pre-commit", "run", "--hook-stage", "pre-push", "--all-files"]`, not `["pre-commit", ...]`. `_is_suite` rejects that argv at the first guard because `_base(head[0]) != "pre-commit"` and `"-m" not in head`; it only accepts an argv[0] basename of `pre-commit` or a `python -m pre_commit...` invocation. As a result, `orphaned_ci_suites()` skips the actual standard-install suite process and `doctor_notes()` never reports the orphan.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/orphan_suites.py:_is_suite

chunk_findings.detail: The `module` predicate is checked without requiring `argv[0]` to be a Python interpreter. It returns true for `argv = ["python", "script.py", "-m", "pre_commit_hooks", "run", "--hook-stage=pre-push", "--all-files"]` because the first four args contain `-m` and a token starting with `pre_commit`, and later args contain `run`, `--hook-stage=pre-push`, and `--all-files`. That process is just `script.py` receiving an `-m` argument, not the pre-commit CLI, so `orphaned_ci_suites` can name an unrelated long-running process as an orphaned suite and `doctor_notes` can suggest killing it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/orphan_suites.py:_is_suite

chunk_findings.detail: The interpreter-script detection only inspects `argv[1]`, so a valid ddflow process launched with an interpreter option before the script path is missed. For example, `python3 -u [REDACTED:path]` gives `rest = ["-u", "[REDACTED:path]"]`; `rest[:1]` is `["-u"]`, no `-m` follows, so `_is_ddflow` returns False. A live ddflow ancestor run this way is then not found in `_has_ddflow_ancestor`, causing active suites under it to be falsely reported as orphaned.

chunk_findings.detail: This new test does not exercise the held-ticket race it is meant to probe, so the previous MEDIUM finding is not answered. `owner_unlinks_while_holding` is a plain function whose `try/finally` unlinks `path` before returning the `fsio.file_lock` context-manager object. Since `fsio.file_lock` is a contextmanager whose `os.open`/`flock` happen when that returned object is entered, the path is gone before the open occurs; `_live` would see a missing-file error, not `fsio.LockTimeout` after the open. Thus the `except fsio.LockTimeout` branch is never reached, and the test passes or fails for a different reason, leaving the original race unverified.
